insular-government-of-the-philippine-isl.t: American civilian colonial government of the Philippines from 1901, which introduced mass schooling and elected Filipino legislatures.
insular-government-of-the-philippine-isl.o: In July 1901 the Philippine Commission led by William Howard Taft took over civil government from the [[s:united-states-military-government-of-the-philippine-islands|United States Military Government of the Philippine Islands]], with Taft as the first civil governor. The Philippine Organic Act of 1902 set its framework, under the Bureau of Insular Affairs in Washington.
insular-government-of-the-philippine-isl.r: The governor-general and commission ruled alongside an elected Philippine Assembly from 1907. American teachers, the Thomasites, spread English-language public schooling, and roads, health services and [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] exports to the [[s:united-states|United States]] grew. The Jones Act of 1916 created an all-Filipino legislature and promised independence, and Governor-General Francis Burton Harrison filled the civil service with Filipinos.
insular-government-of-the-philippine-isl.e: Campaigns by Manuel Quezon and Sergio Osmena led to the Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934, and in November 1935 the Insular Government was replaced by the [[s:commonwealth-of-the-philippines|Commonwealth of the Philippines]] as a transition to independence.

ialysos.t: One of the three ancient cities of Rhodes, on the hill of Philerimos, home of the famous Olympic boxing family of Diagoras.
ialysos.o: Ialysos lay on the north-west coast of [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]], below Mount Philerimos. A Minoan and then Mycenaean settlement flourished there, with rich chamber tombs. In the early Iron Age Dorian [[e:greeks|Greeks]] settled, and Ialysos became one of the three cities of [[e:rhodes|Rhodes]], with [[s:lindos|Lindos]] and [[s:kamiros|Kamiros]], in the Dorian Hexapolis.
ialysos.r: The city's acropolis sanctuary of Athena and Zeus Polieus stood on Philerimos. Ialysos took part in Rhodian trade and colonisation, and came under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] before joining the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. Its leading family, the Diagorids, produced Olympic champions, including the boxer Diagoras, celebrated by Pindar in 464 BCE.
ialysos.e: In 408 BCE Ialysos joined [[s:lindos|Lindos]] and [[s:kamiros|Kamiros]] to found the city of [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]], which absorbed its political life. Ialysos continued as a religious centre and later hosted a Byzantine fortress and a monastery of the Knights of [[s:hospitaller-rhodes|Hospitaller Rhodes]].

islamic-state-of-medina.t: The first Muslim community-state, founded by Muhammad at Medina in 622, which united most of Arabia within a decade.
islamic-state-of-medina.o: In 622 Muhammad and his followers left [[e:mecca|Mecca]] for Yathrib, later called [[e:medina|Medina]], at the invitation of its feuding Arab tribes. This migration, the [[e:hijra|Hijra]], became the start of the [[e:islamic-calendar|Islamic calendar]]. The document known as the Constitution of Medina bound the emigrants, the local Muslims and the Jewish tribes into a single community, the umma.
islamic-state-of-medina.r: Muhammad acted as prophet, judge and military leader. Revelations of the [[e:quran|Quran]] in this period set out rules on prayer, fasting, alms, marriage and inheritance. The community fought [[s:pre-islamic-mecca|Pre-Islamic Mecca]] at Badr (624), Uhud (625) and the Trench (627), and expelled or defeated the Jewish tribes of [[e:medina|Medina]]. The Treaty of Hudaybiyya in 628 brought a truce.
islamic-state-of-medina.e: [[e:mecca|Mecca]] surrendered in 630, and delegations from across [[e:arabia|Arabia]] submitted in the following two years. When Muhammad died in 632, Abu Bakr was chosen as his successor, founding the [[s:rashidun-caliphate|Rashidun Caliphate]]. [[e:medina|Medina]] remained its capital and is the second holiest city of [[e:islam|Islam]].

imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.t: A Premonstratensian abbey in upper Swabia, famed for its rococo library hall, whose abbots ruled a small imperial territory.
imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.o: Founded in 1183 by the lords of Schussenried as a house of Premonstratensian canons, the community was raised to an abbey in 1440. Its abbots gradually freed themselves from outside advocates, gaining imperial immediacy and a seat among the Swabian prelates of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.r: The abbot ruled several villages in upper Swabia as a member of the Swabian Circle, supported by farms, forests and tithes. The abbey commissioned the pilgrimage church of Steinhausen, built by Dominikus Zimmermann from 1728, and in the 18th century began a grand new monastery whose library hall, painted by Franz Georg Hermann, is a masterpiece of rococo.
imperial-abbey-of-schussenried.e: Secularised in 1803, Schussenried was granted to the counts of Sternberg-Manderscheid and passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806. The library hall survives in Bad Schussenried.

idumea.t: Small Livonian-Latgalian district in northern Latvia where the chronicler Henry of Livonia served as a parish priest.
idumea.o: Idumea lay north of the Gauja river, between the Liv lands of [[s:turaida|Turaida]] and [[s:metsepole|Metsepole]] and the Latgalian land of [[s:talava|Tālava]]. Its population was mixed Livonian and Latgalian, and it appears in Henry of [[e:livonia|Livonia's]] chronicle in the early 13th century.
idumea.r: Its people lived in small farming communities under local elders. After the Germans arrived they accepted baptism, and Henry himself, the author of the chronicle, was ordained and served as priest among the Idumeans from about 1208.
idumea.e: Idumea came under the [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Riga around 1206 and became part of the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]] and [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]]. Its people were absorbed into the Latvian population.
idumea.re: Baltic and Finnic paganism, later Christianity

insubres.t: Celtic people of the Po plain who founded Milan and were the strongest Gaulish opponents of Rome in northern Italy.
insubres.o: Livy says Celts led by Bellovesus crossed the [[e:alps|Alps]] around 600 BCE and founded Mediolanum, the later [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]], on land already called Insubrian. Archaeology shows the local Golasecca culture, which already spoke a Celtic language, Lepontic, absorbing larger Gaulish migrations in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE.
insubres.r: The Insubres formed a tribal state with Mediolanum as a central place, ruled by warrior aristocrats and kings. They lived in villages and fortified centres, farmed the rich plain and minted [[e:silver|silver]] coins imitating those of [[s:massalia|Massalia]]. They often led the Cisalpine [[e:gauls|Gauls]] in war, joining the [[s:boii|Boii]] against [[e:rome|Rome]] in 225 BCE.
insubres.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] defeated them at Telamon in 225 BCE and at Clastidium in 222 BCE, and took Mediolanum. They backed [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]], but after defeats in 196 and 194 BCE they accepted a treaty. Their land was gradually Romanised, gaining [[e:latin|Latin]] and then full citizenship in the 1st century BCE.

imperial-abbey-of-werden.t: A Benedictine abbey on the Ruhr founded by the missionary Saint Ludger, which ruled a small imperial territory for a thousand years.
imperial-abbey-of-werden.o: Saint Ludger, a Frisian missionary and later first [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Münster, founded a monastery at Werden on the Ruhr around 799 on land he had acquired. He was buried there in 809, and his family's abbots ran the house for decades. In 877 it became a royal abbey under imperial protection.
imperial-abbey-of-werden.r: Werden held estates from Frisia to the Rhineland, and its abbots ruled the area around Werden as princes of the Empire. Its library held the Codex Argenteus, the [[e:silver|silver]] Bible of the Gothic language, before it passed to [[e:prague|Prague]] and later Uppsala. The protectors of the abbey were the counts of the Mark and later the rulers of Brandenburg-[[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]].
imperial-abbey-of-werden.e: Werden remained a Catholic island but a small one. In 1803 the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss secularised it and gave it to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. Its Romanesque church, the basilica of Saint Ludger, survives in what is now a district of Essen.

islamic-state-of-afghanistan.t: The mujahideen government that took Kabul in 1992 and fought a ruinous civil war, remaining the internationally recognised government even after the Taliban won.
islamic-state-of-afghanistan.o: After the fall of Mohammad Najibullah's government of the [[s:democratic-republic-of-afghanistan|Democratic Republic of Afghanistan]] in April 1992, mujahideen parties agreed in the [[e:peshawar|Peshawar]] Accord to form the Islamic State of [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-2021-present|Afghanistan]]. Sibghatullah Mojaddedi served briefly as president, followed by Burhanuddin Rabbani of the Jamiat-e Islami.
islamic-state-of-afghanistan.r: The government, with Ahmad Shah Massoud as defence minister, never controlled the country. Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-e Islami, Abdul Rashid Dostum's [[e:uzbeks|Uzbek]] militia and the [[e:hazara|Hazara]] Hezb-e Wahdat fought each other and the government for [[e:kabul|Kabul]], killing tens of thousands of civilians in shelling. Regional warlords ruled elsewhere, and the country fragmented.
islamic-state-of-afghanistan.e: The Taliban took [[e:kabul|Kabul]] in 1996, founding the [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001|Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan]] (1996-2001). Rabbani's government kept the UN seat and controlled the north-east through the [[s:ouetsu-reppan-domei|Northern Alliance]]. After the US-led intervention of 2001, Rabbani handed power to the [[s:islamic-republic-of-afghanistan|Islamic Republic of Afghanistan]]'s interim administration.

imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.t: The territory taken by the German Empire from France in 1871, governed directly from Berlin until it returned to France in 1918.
imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.o: By the Treaty of [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] of 1871, which ended the [[e:franco-prussian-war|Franco-Prussian War]], [[e:france|France]] ceded Alsace and part of [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]], including Metz, to the new [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. Instead of joining an existing state, the region became a Reichsland, an imperial territory under the emperor's direct authority.
imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.r: The territory was administered from Berlin and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]], and from 1879 by an imperial governor (Statthalter) in Strasbourg, the first being Edwin von Manteuffel. Tens of thousands opted for French citizenship and left. [[e:germany|Germany]] invested in Strasbourg's university and new imperial quarter. A constitution of 1911 created a regional parliament, but the Saverne Affair of 1913, when soldiers abused civilians, revealed lasting tensions.
imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine.e: After [[e:germany|Germany's]] defeat in November 1918, councils briefly proclaimed the [[s:republic-of-alsace-lorraine|Republic of Alsace-Lorraine]] before French troops entered. The [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]] of 1919 returned the territory to [[e:france|France]], where it still keeps some distinct local laws.

imamate-of-nasir-al-din.t: A short-lived Islamic reform movement led by the Berber scholar Nasir al-Din, which overthrew the kings of the lower Senegal valley in the 1670s.
imamate-of-nasir-al-din.o: Nasir al-Din was a cleric of the Zawaya, the [[e:berbers|Berber]] scholarly tribes of south-western [[e:mauritania|Mauritania]], who resented the dominance of Hassani Arab warriors and the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] with the French at Saint-Louis. Around 1673 he proclaimed a holy war, known as the Tubenan movement, calling for rule by Islamic law.
imamate-of-nasir-al-din.r: His followers overthrew or converted the rulers of [[s:waalo|Waalo]], [[s:cayor|Kayor]], the [[s:kingdom-of-jolof|Kingdom of Jolof]] and [[s:imamate-of-futa-toro|Futa Toro]], replacing them with clerics loyal to the [[e:imam|imam]]. The movement drew on peasant grievances against kings who sold their subjects into [[e:slavery|slavery]]. Nasir al-Din was killed in battle against Hassani warriors in 1674.
imamate-of-nasir-al-din.e: Under his successors the movement weakened. The old ruling families, supported by the French, regained their thrones by 1677, and the Hassani defeated the Zawaya in the Char Bouba war. The idea of a clerical state inspired later [[e:fula|Fulani]] revolutions in [[s:imamate-of-futa-jallon|Futa Jallon]] and [[s:imamate-of-futa-toro|Futa Toro]].

imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.t: A Premonstratensian abbey on the Danube in upper Swabia whose abbots ruled a small territory of villages until 1803.
imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.o: A collegiate foundation existed at Marchtal from the 8th century, and in 1171 [[e:count-palatine|Count Palatine]] Hugh of Tübingen refounded it for Premonstratensian canons. Raised to an abbey in 1440, it gained imperial immediacy around 1500, and its abbot sat on the Swabian bench of prelates.
imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.r: The abbot governed several villages along the [[e:danube|Danube]] and in the hills nearby. Between 1686 and 1701 the canons built a large new church, designed by the Vorarlberg masters Michael and Christian Thumb, one of the earliest great Baroque churches of upper Swabia. The abbey remained Catholic.
imperial-abbey-of-marchtal.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and given to the princes of [[s:principality-of-thurn-and-taxis|Thurn und Taxis]], who used the buildings as a residence. The territory passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806, and the former abbey now belongs to the diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart.

imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.t: An island abbey on Lake Constance and one of the great centres of Carolingian and Ottonian learning and book painting, now a World Heritage Site.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.o: In 724 the wandering [[e:bishop|bishop]] Pirmin founded a Benedictine monastery on the island of Reichenau in Lake Constance, with the support of [[e:charles-martel|Charles Martel]]. It quickly became one of the leading abbeys of the Frankish realm, receiving estates across Alamannia and close links with the Carolingian court.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.r: Reichenau flourished in the 9th to 11th centuries: Abbot Walafrid Strabo wrote his poem on gardening, the Hortulus, there; the abbey library was among the largest in [[e:europe|Europe]]; and its scriptorium produced Ottonian illuminated [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]] for emperors. Its abbots were imperial princes who ruled a small territory around the lake.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.e: The abbey declined from the 13th century as its income fell and its noble-only admissions shrank the community. In 1540 it was incorporated into the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-constance|Prince-Bishopric of Constance]], whose [[e:bishop|bishops]] became its abbots. It was secularised in 1803; its churches at Oberzell, Mittelzell and Niederzell survive.
imperial-abbey-of-reichenau.la: Latin, Old and Middle High German

ionian-league.t: Religious and political union of twelve Ionian cities on the coast of Anatolia, centred on the Panionion, which led the Ionian Revolt against Persia.
ionian-league.o: The twelve cities were [[s:miletus|Miletus]], [[s:myus|Myus]], [[s:priene|Priene]], [[s:ephesus|Ephesus]], [[s:colophon|Colophon]], [[s:lebedos|Lebedos]], [[s:teos|Teos]], [[s:clazomenae|Clazomenae]], [[s:phocaea|Phocaea]], [[s:samos|Samos]], [[s:chios|Chios]] and [[s:erythrae|Erythrae]]; [[s:smyrna|Smyrna]] joined later. They formed the league c. 700 BCE, after destroying the city of Melia, whose land became the site of the Panionion, a shrine of Poseidon Helikonios on Mount Mycale.
ionian-league.r: The league held the Panionia festival and met to discuss common affairs, but the cities stayed independent and often fought each other. Thales proposed a single council at [[s:teos|Teos]], and Bias of [[s:priene|Priene]] urged mass emigration to [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]] when [[e:persia|Persia]] attacked c. 545 BCE; neither advice was followed. The cities fell to the [[s:kingdom-of-lydia|Kingdom of Lydia]] and the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]].
ionian-league.e: Delegates met at the Panionion to coordinate the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE, which ended with defeat at Lade and the sack of [[s:miletus|Miletus]] in 494 BCE. The league survived later only as a religious association.
ionian-league.re: Greek religion; cult of Poseidon Helikonios

ile-royale.t: France's colony on Cape Breton Island, built around the fortress town of Louisbourg to guard the approaches to the St Lawrence after 1713.
ile-royale.o: The [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] of 1713 gave [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] the peninsula of [[s:acadia|Acadia]] and [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]] but left [[e:france|France]] [[s:colony-of-cape-breton-island|Cape Breton]] Island, renamed Ile Royale, and Ile Saint-Jean, now [[s:colony-of-prince-edward-island|Prince Edward Island]]. French settlers from [[s:plaisance|Plaisance]] moved there, and from 1719 the Crown built the fortified town of Louisbourg on the east coast.
ile-royale.r: Louisbourg, with massive stone walls in the style of Vauban, was the colony's capital, garrison and port. The economy rested on the cod fishery, which made Ile Royale one of [[e:france|France's]] most valuable colonies, and on trade with France, the West Indies, [[s:province-of-quebec|Quebec]] and even New [[e:england|England]]. Governors such as Joseph de Saint-Ovide de Brouillan ran a society of soldiers, merchants and fishermen.
ile-royale.e: New [[e:england|England]] forces captured Louisbourg in 1745, but it was returned in 1748. The British took it again in 1758, demolished the fortifications in 1760, and the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1763 ceded the island to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. Louisbourg was partly rebuilt in the 1960s.

imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.t: A noble women's convent founded by the ancestors of the Ottonian emperors, home of Hrotsvitha, the first known German woman poet and playwright.
imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.o: The [[e:saxons|Saxon]] count Liudolf and his wife Oda founded a convent in 852 at Brunshausen, which moved to Gandersheim in 856. Their daughter Hathumod was the first abbess. As the family monastery of the Liudolfings, who became the Ottonian kings, it enjoyed royal favour, and in 919 it was made a royal abbey.
imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.r: Gandersheim was a community of canonesses, mostly from high noble families, ruled by an abbess who became a princess of the Empire. Around 960 the canoness Hrotsvitha wrote [[e:latin|Latin]] plays, legends and verse histories of [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] there. The abbey ruled a small territory around Bad Gandersheim under the protection of the dukes of Brunswick.
imperial-abbey-of-gandersheim.e: Gandersheim accepted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1560s, becoming a Lutheran foundation under the Brunswick dukes. It lost its imperial status with secularisation in 1802 to 1803, passing to Brunswick, and the convent was dissolved in 1810 under the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]].

ile-bourbon.t: France's Indian Ocean island colony of Bourbon, built on coffee, sugar and slavery, which became the department of Reunion in 1946.
ile-bourbon.o: [[e:france|France]] claimed the uninhabited island in 1642 and named it [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbon]] after the royal house in 1649. Permanent settlement began in 1665 when the [[e:french-east-india-company|French East India Company]] sent Etienne Regnault as commandant with a small group of colonists, joined by survivors from the [[s:fort-dauphin-colony|Fort-Dauphin Colony]].
ile-bourbon.r: From 1715 the Company introduced [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], and the island became a plantation society worked by enslaved people from Madagascar, [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]] and [[e:india|India]]. Mahe de La Bourdonnais governed it together with [[s:isle-de-france|Isle de France]] in the 1730s and 1740s. Renamed Reunion in 1793, the island was occupied by [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from 1810 to 1815; [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] replaced coffee and [[e:slavery|slavery]] was abolished in 1848, followed by indentured labour.
ile-bourbon.e: [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbon]], by then known again as Reunion, remained a French colony until 1946, when it became an overseas [[e:departement|department]] of [[e:france|France]], a status it still holds.

imperial-abbey-of-prum.t: A great Carolingian abbey in the Eifel, the burial place of Emperor Lothair I and a rich imperial territory until Trier absorbed it.
imperial-abbey-of-prum.o: The abbey was founded in 721 by Bertrada the Elder, and refounded in 752 by her grandson Pippin the Short and his wife Bertrada of Laon, who gave it rich estates. Under Carolingian favour Prüm became one of the most important monasteries between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the Meuse.
imperial-abbey-of-prum.r: The Prüm Urbar of 893, a register of estates and dues, is a key source on the Carolingian rural economy. Abbot Regino of Prüm wrote an important chronicle there, and Emperor [[e:lothair-i|Lothair I]] retired to the abbey and died there in 855. Later its abbot was a prince of the Empire ruling a small territory in the Eifel.
imperial-abbey-of-prum.e: Prüm's possessions shrank from the 13th century, and the archbishops of [[e:trier|Trier]] sought control over it. In 1576 the abbey was incorporated into the [[s:electorate-of-trier|Electorate of Trier]], the archbishop acting as its administrator. The monastery itself survived until French secularisation in 1802.

italian-social-republic.t: The Fascist puppet state set up by Nazi Germany in northern Italy in 1943, with Mussolini at its head, which collapsed in April 1945.
italian-social-republic.o: After the [[s:kingdom-of-italy|Kingdom of Italy]] signed an [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] with the [[e:allies|Allies]] in September 1943, German forces occupied northern and central [[e:italy|Italy]]. German paratroopers freed [[e:benito-mussolini|Mussolini]] from captivity on the Gran Sasso, and he proclaimed a new Fascist state, with ministries scattered around Lake Garda, especially at Salò.
italian-social-republic.r: The republic depended entirely on German forces, who controlled the economy and deported Italian [[e:jews|Jews]] and workers. Its [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]] Manifesto of 1943 promised a socialist-style programme, and the Verona trial of January 1944 executed Galeazzo Ciano and others who had voted against [[e:benito-mussolini|Mussolini]]. Its militias and the Germans waged a bitter war against the partisan resistance, with reprisals against civilians.
italian-social-republic.e: The Allied offensive and a general partisan uprising in April 1945 brought collapse. [[e:benito-mussolini|Mussolini]] was captured while fleeing towards [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] and shot on 28 April 1945, and the German forces in [[e:italy|Italy]] surrendered on 2 May.

imperial-abbey-of-essen.t: A royal convent for noble women whose princess-abbesses ruled the town of Essen and whose treasure includes the oldest surviving statue of the Virgin Mary.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.o: Essen Abbey was founded around 845 to 852 by Altfrid, later [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Hildesheim, as a community of canonesses for women of the [[e:saxons|Saxon]] nobility. It received royal protection and immunity, and under the Ottonians it became a favoured house of the ruling dynasty.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.r: The abbesses Mathilde, a granddaughter of [[e:otto-i|Otto I]], and Theophanu, granddaughter of Otto II, made Essen a centre of Ottonian art; the Golden Madonna of about 980 and the Otto-Mathilde Cross belong to its treasury. The abbess was a princess of the Empire with a seat in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]], and ruled the small territory around Essen, often in conflict with the town.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.e: Essen was secularised in 1803 and passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]; the last abbess was Maria Kunigunde of Saxony. The town grew into the centre of Ruhr industry, and the former abbey church became Essen Cathedral when the diocese was founded in 1958.
imperial-abbey-of-essen.la: Old Saxon, Middle Low German, Latin

ile-sainte-marie.t: An island off Madagascar's east coast that went from pirate haven to French outpost, ceded to France in 1750.
ile-sainte-marie.o: In the 1690s Ile Sainte-Marie (Nosy Boraha) became a base for [[e:piracy|pirates]] raiding the [[e:indian-ocean|Indian Ocean]], with a trading post run by Adam Baldridge supplying them. Descendants of the pirates and local Malagasy later formed part of the [[s:betsimisaraka-confederation|Betsimisaraka Confederation]]. In 1750 Princess Bety, daughter of Ratsimilaho, ceded the island to [[e:france|France]].
ile-sainte-marie.r: The [[e:french-east-india-company|French East India Company]] established a small post, but disease and a Malagasy uprising soon forced its abandonment. [[e:france|France]] reoccupied the island in 1818 under Sylvain Roux, building at Ambodifotatra a base for trade and for French claims on Madagascar. It was administered from [[s:ile-bourbon|Ile Bourbon]] for much of the 19th century, with a small Catholic population.
ile-sainte-marie.e: In 1896 Sainte-Marie was attached to the new French colony of Madagascar, and it has been part of Madagascar since independence in 1960.

iraca.t: A Muisca priestly lordship centred on Sugamuxi, home of the great Temple of the Sun and chosen as the sacred heart of the Muisca world.
iraca.o: Iraca, centred on Sugamuxi, the modern Sogamoso in Boyacá, was one of the territories of the [[s:muisca-confederation|Muisca Confederation]]. Muisca tradition held that the culture hero Bochica, also called Idacansas, had lived there and named his successor before departing, making Sugamuxi a sacred place.
iraca.r: Iraca was ruled by a high priest, the iraca, who was chosen alternately from two local communities, Tobasá and Firavitoba, and confirmed by nearby chiefs. The Temple of the Sun at Sugamuxi drew pilgrims and offerings. Iraca stood apart from the rival zaque of [[s:zacazgo-of-hunza|Hunza]] and the zipa of [[s:zipazgo-of-bacata|Bacatá]] and was often allied with [[s:tundama|Tundama]].
iraca.e: Spanish troops under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada reached Sugamuxi in 1537, and the Temple of the Sun burned down while soldiers looted it. Iraca was then absorbed into the [[s:new-kingdom-of-granada|New Kingdom of Granada]]. The temple has been reconstructed in Sogamoso's archaeological museum.

imperial-abbey-of-herford.t: A convent for noble women in Westphalia whose abbesses ruled as princesses of the Empire for a thousand years.
imperial-abbey-of-herford.o: Herford Abbey was founded around 789 by a [[e:saxons|Saxon]] noble named Waltger as a community of women, soon after [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] conquest of Saxony. Under [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]] it became a royal abbey, and it was among the oldest women's foundations in Saxony. Queen Matilda, wife of Henry the Fowler, was educated there.
imperial-abbey-of-herford.r: Herford was a secular canonesses' foundation for daughters of the high nobility. Its abbess was a princess of the Empire with a seat in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]]. The town of Herford grew around the abbey and joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]]. In the 17th century Princess Elisabeth of the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]], correspondent of Descartes, was abbess.
imperial-abbey-of-herford.e: The town and abbey accepted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], the abbey becoming Lutheran, but its princely status remained under the protection of Brandenburg-[[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. Herford's imperial status ended with secularisation in 1803, when its lands passed to Prussia. The convent was formally dissolved in 1810.

imperial-british-east-africa-company.t: A chartered British trading company that governed much of Kenya and Uganda in the race for East Africa before handing it to the Crown.
imperial-british-east-africa-company.o: The company was founded by the Scottish shipping [[e:magnates|magnate]] William Mackinnon and received a royal charter in 1888, following the Anglo-German agreement of 1886 that divided spheres of influence in [[e:east-africa|East Africa]]. It leased the coastal strip from the [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Sultanate of Zanzibar]] and aimed to open trade routes to the [[e:great-lakes|Great Lakes]].
imperial-british-east-africa-company.r: With few resources, the company built forts along the caravan route inland and relied on treaties with local leaders. Its agent [[e:frederick-lugard|Frederick Lugard]] reached the [[s:kingdom-of-buganda|Kingdom of Buganda]] in 1890, made a treaty with Kabaka Mwanga II and intervened in the conflict between Protestant and Catholic factions. The company also restored the [[s:kingdom-of-toro|Kingdom of Toro]]. Trade proved unprofitable and costs mounted.
imperial-british-east-africa-company.e: The company could not afford its commitments, and the British government took over: the [[s:uganda-protectorate|Uganda Protectorate]] was declared in 1894 and the [[s:east-africa-protectorate|East Africa Protectorate]] in 1895, when the company surrendered its charter in return for compensation.

imamate-of-aussa.t: The last refuge of the old Adal state, moved from Harar to the Aussa oasis in the Afar lowlands to escape Oromo attacks.
imamate-of-aussa.o: After the death of [[e:ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi|Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi]] and decades of war, the [[s:adal-sultanate|Adal Sultanate]] was weakened by [[e:oromo|Oromo]] raids on [[e:harar|Harar]]. In 1577 [[e:imam|Imam]] Muhammad Jasa moved the seat of government to the oasis of Aussa on the lower Awash river, in the [[e:afar|Afar]] lowlands, creating a new [[e:imamate|imamate]] there.
imamate-of-aussa.r: The [[e:imam|imams]] claimed to continue Adal's religious leadership but ruled a much smaller state, dependent on the irrigated farmland of the Aussa oasis and on [[e:afar|Afar]] pastoralists. [[e:harar|Harar]] was left under its own governors. Raids by [[e:oromo|Oromo]] and Afar groups and disputes over succession kept the [[e:imamate|imamate]] weak.
imamate-of-aussa.e: The [[e:imamate|imamate]] disintegrated in the later 17th century, with the [[e:imam|imams]] reduced to figureheads and finally overthrown, traditionally around 1672. In 1734 the [[e:afar|Afar]] Mudaito clan founded the [[s:aussa-sultanate|Aussa Sultanate]] on its former lands, while [[e:harar|Harar]] became the separate [[s:harar-emirate|Harar Emirate]].

imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.t: Premonstratensian abbey near Ravensburg that ruled a small Swabian territory as an imperial prelacy and built a grand baroque church.
imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.o: The abbey was founded in 1145 by Gebizo of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg|Ravensburg]], a ministerial of the Guelphs, and settled by Premonstratensian canons. It lay on the Schussen just south of Ravensburg. With Hohenstaufen and later royal protection it gained imperial immediacy in the 13th century, around 1257.
imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.r: The abbots, elected by the canons, ruled villages, farms and forests around the abbey and sat on the bench of Swabian imperial prelates in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]]. Their territory was small and rural, and they defended their rights against the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg|Free Imperial City of Ravensburg]] and the [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] bailiwick. In the early 18th century the abbey rebuilt its church in baroque style.
imperial-abbey-of-weissenau.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and given to the counts of Sternberg-Manderscheid as compensation for lands lost to [[e:france|France]], and in 1806 it passed to Württemberg. Its church survives as a parish church in [[s:free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg|Ravensburg]].

imperial-abbey-of-murbach.t: A wealthy Alsatian abbey whose abbots were princes of the Empire, ruling a small Vosges territory until the French Revolution swept it away.
imperial-abbey-of-murbach.o: Murbach Abbey was founded in 727 in a valley of the southern Vosges by Saint Pirmin, with the support of the Alsatian duke Eberhard of the Etichonid family. It soon became one of the richest monasteries of Alsace, with estates stretching into Swabia and [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]], including the town of [[s:canton-of-lucerne|Lucerne]], which it held until 1291.
imperial-abbey-of-murbach.r: The abbots became princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], ruling Guebwiller and the surrounding valleys. Only nobles could join the community. In 1560 Murbach was united with the Abbey of Lure. After [[e:france|France]] gained Alsace in 1648, the princely abbots kept their rights under French [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]]. The Romanesque abbey church still stands.
imperial-abbey-of-murbach.e: The monks, wearied by the remote valley, moved to Guebwiller, and in 1764 the abbey became a secular collegiate chapter. During the French Revolution in 1789 the chapter's lands were seized and its palaces in Guebwiller looted, ending more than a thousand years of ecclesiastical lordship.

itanos.t: Port city of far eastern Crete, involved in the founding of Cyrene and long locked in disputes over the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus.
itanos.o: Itanos lay on a bay at the north-east tip of [[e:crete|Crete]], near Cape Sideros, and was settled in the early Iron Age, possibly with Phoenician involvement. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] tells that Corobius, a purple-fisher from Itanos, guided the Therans to [[e:libya|Libya]] before they founded [[s:republic-of-cyrene|Cyrene]] c. 631 BCE.
itanos.r: Itanos lived from fishing, purple dye and trade, with coins showing sea creatures. It had a long-running dispute with [[s:praisos|Praisos]] and later [[s:hierapytna|Hierapytna]] over the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus at Palaikastro and the land around it. In the 3rd century BCE it hosted a Ptolemaic garrison, which protected it against its neighbours.
itanos.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] arbitrated the [[s:hierapytna|Hierapytna]] dispute through Magnesia c. 112 BCE. Itanos was absorbed into Roman [[e:crete|Crete]] after 67 BCE and was abandoned in the Byzantine period.
itanos.re: Greek religion; cult of Diktaean Zeus

illinois-confederation.t: An alliance of Algonquian peoples of the upper Mississippi valley, close partners of the French, whose name lives on in the state of Illinois.
illinois-confederation.o: The Illinois, or Inoka, were a group of a dozen or more related peoples, among them the Kaskaskia, Peoria, [[s:cahokia|Cahokia]], Tamaroa and Michigamea, who lived along the Illinois and middle [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] rivers by the 17th century. When Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet visited in 1673, the Grand Village of the Kaskaskia near Starved Rock held thousands of people.
illinois-confederation.r: Each tribe had its own village chiefs, with war and peace chiefs, and the confederation shared language, ceremonies and alliances. The Illinois farmed [[e:maize|maize]] and hunted bison on the prairies in seasonal expeditions. Allied with [[s:new-france|New France]], they hosted [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missions and French settlements such as Kaskaskia and [[s:cahokia|Cahokia]], and many became Catholic. Iroquois attacks in 1680 and wars with the Fox, Sauk and others reduced their numbers.
illinois-confederation.e: Epidemics, alcohol and war shrank the Illinois from perhaps 10,000 to a few hundred by 1800. After the killing of the Ottawa leader Pontiac by a Peoria in 1769, enemies attacked them. They ceded their lands in treaties ending in 1832 and moved west; descendants form the Peoria Tribe of Oklahoma.

itza-kingdom-of-nojpeten.t: The last independent Maya kingdom, ruled from the island city of Nojpetén in Lake Petén Itzá until its conquest by Spain in 1697.
itza-kingdom-of-nojpeten.o: The Itza claimed descent from the rulers of [[s:chichen-itza|Chichen Itza]] and said they migrated south to the Petén lakes after its decline. By the mid-15th century, around 1440, they had established a kingdom with its capital on the island of Nojpetén, where Flores stands today.
itza-kingdom-of-nojpeten.r: The Itza were ruled by a king titled Ajaw Kan Ek', who shared power with a high priest and a council of lords representing four quarters. Nojpetén had temples and houses covering the island, and the kingdom controlled much of the central Petén. [[e:hernan-cortes|Hernán Cortés]] visited in 1525, and for 170 years the Itza resisted missionaries and soldiers, sheltered by forest and distance.
itza-kingdom-of-nojpeten.e: After Franciscan missions and failed negotiations, Martín de Ursúa stormed Nojpetén by boat on 13 March 1697 and destroyed its temples. The Itza kingdom ended, though its people fled into the forest. Itza Maya is still spoken by a few around the lake.

islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001.t: The first Taliban regime, which imposed a severe Islamic order on Afghanistan and sheltered al-Qaeda until the US-led invasion of 2001.
islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001.o: The Taliban movement arose in [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] in 1994 among religious students led by Mullah Mohammad Omar, promising to end the warlordism of the [[s:islamic-state-of-afghanistan|Islamic State of Afghanistan]]. With support from [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]], it took Kandahar in 1994, [[e:herat|Herat]] in 1995 and [[e:kabul|Kabul]] in September 1996, proclaiming the Islamic [[e:emirate|Emirate]].
islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001.r: Mullah Omar ruled as [[e:commander-of-the-faithful|Amir al-Mu'minin]] from [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]]. The regime enforced a strict interpretation of [[e:sharia|sharia]], banning girls' education and most women's employment, music and television. It controlled about 90 per cent of the country but was recognised only by [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]], [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]] and the UAE. In March 2001 it destroyed the Buddhas of Bamiyan. It hosted Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.
islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001.e: After the attacks of 11 September 2001, the Taliban refused to hand over bin Laden. A US-led coalition and the [[s:ouetsu-reppan-domei|Northern Alliance]] overthrew the regime by December 2001, and the [[s:islamic-republic-of-afghanistan|Islamic Republic of Afghanistan]] was established. The Taliban regrouped and fought an insurgency for twenty years.

imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.t: One of Bavaria's oldest Benedictine abbeys, which became an imperial principality of its own inside the walls of Regensburg.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.o: The abbey grew up in the 8th century over the tomb of Saint Emmeram, a Frankish [[e:bishop|bishop]] martyred around 652, and for long its abbots were also bishops of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]]. It separated from the bishopric in 975 under Saint Wolfgang. Its independence from Bavarian and episcopal control was confirmed by the king in 1295, and in 1731 its abbots were raised to princes of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.r: The prince-abbot sat in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]], which from 1663 met permanently in [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]], yet his territory was little more than the abbey precinct and a few estates. Saint Emmeram was famous for its scriptorium and library, which held the Codex Aureus of Saint Emmeram, and in the 18th century for scientific scholarship. It remained Catholic within a Lutheran free city, the Free Imperial City of Regensburg.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-emmeram.e: In 1803 the abbey passed to the short-lived Principality of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]] under Karl Theodor von Dalberg; the monastery was dissolved after Regensburg went to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]] in 1810. In 1812 the buildings became the residence of the princes of [[s:principality-of-thurn-and-taxis|Thurn und Taxis]], who still live there.

ituraea.t: Ituraea, an Arab principality of the Beqaa valley and Mount Lebanon, known for its archers and its brigandage.
ituraea.o: The Ituraeans, an Arab people, took control of the Beqaa valley and parts of Mount [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]] and the Hermon in the late 2nd century BCE, as the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]] declined. Their ruler Ptolemy son of Mennaeus governed from [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]] and extended power towards [[e:damascus|Damascus]] and the coast.
ituraea.r: Ituraean rulers were also high priests of a local cult, and their warriors were renowned [[e:archery|archers]] later serving in Roman armies. Strabo describes them as brigands raiding the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]]. Ptolemy made peace with [[e:pompey|Pompey]] in 64 BCE and kept his principality as a Roman client.
ituraea.e: Ptolemy's son Lysanias was executed by [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony]] in 36 BCE. Augustus took lands from the tetrarch Zenodorus and gave them to the [[s:herodian-kingdom-of-judea|Herodian Kingdom of Judea]] in 20 BCE, and Ituraea was divided among neighbours.

illyrian-provinces.t: French-ruled provinces on the Adriatic created by Napoleon, which brought modern administration and an early taste of South Slav unity.
illyrian-provinces.o: After defeating [[e:austria|Austria]], [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] took Carniola, western Carinthia, Gorizia, Trieste, [[s:histria|Istria]] and Croatia south of the Sava under the Treaty of Schönbrunn in 1809. He joined them with [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]], [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]] and the Bay of [[s:commune-of-kotor|Kotor]], already in French hands, to form the Illyrian Provinces, cutting Austria off from the sea.
illyrian-provinces.r: A governor-general in Ljubljana, first Marshal Auguste de Marmont, ruled under French law, abolishing many feudal dues, building roads and opening schools teaching in Slovene and Croatian. The poet Valentin Vodnik celebrated the change in Illyria Revived. [[e:conscription|Conscription]], heavy taxes and the Continental [[e:naval-blockade|Blockade]], which ruined Adriatic trade, made French rule unpopular.
illyrian-provinces.e: Austrian troops recovered the provinces in 1813, and they were formally dissolved in 1816, when most became the [[s:kingdom-of-illyria|Kingdom of Illyria]] and [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]] a separate kingdom. The name Illyria inspired the Croatian Illyrian movement of the 1830s.

ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.t: A brief Ibadi revolt-state that rose in Hadramawt, took Sanaa, Mecca and Medina, and was destroyed by the last Umayyad caliph.
ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.o: In 746, as the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] was torn by civil war, the Kindite judge Abd Allah ibn Yahya, known as Talib al-Haqq, was proclaimed [[e:imam|imam]] by Ibadi missionaries from [[e:basra|Basra]] in [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]]. He quickly took Sanaa and became master of most of [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]].
ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.r: The [[e:imamate|imamate]] followed Ibadi principles of an elected, accountable [[e:imam|imam]] and avoided plunder and indiscriminate killing of opponents. In 747 his general Abu Hamza al-Mukhtar ibn Awf marched north, appeared at the pilgrimage, defeated an Umayyad army at Qudayd and occupied [[e:mecca|Mecca]] and [[e:medina|Medina]], where his sermons were long remembered.
ibadi-imamate-of-hadramawt.e: [[e:marwan-ii|Marwan II]] sent Abd al-Malik ibn Atiyya with Syrian troops. He defeated Abu Hamza in the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Hejaz]] in 747, then pursued Talib al-Haqq, who was killed in battle; by 748 [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] was recovered. Ibadi activity continued in [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]] and inspired the [[s:first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman|First Ibadi Imamate of Oman]].

italian-regency-of-carnaro.t: Poet Gabriele D'Annunzio's self-proclaimed state in Fiume, a theatrical experiment that foreshadowed the style and rituals of Italian Fascism.
italian-regency-of-carnaro.o: After the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], [[e:italy|Italy]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]] both claimed the port of [[s:free-state-of-fiume|Fiume]], today Rijeka, which had an Italian-speaking majority in the town. On 12 September 1919 the nationalist poet Gabriele D'Annunzio led some 2,600 [[e:legion|legionaries]] into Fiume and occupied it in defiance of the Italian government. In September 1920 he proclaimed the Italian Regency of Carnaro.
italian-regency-of-carnaro.r: Its constitution, the Charter of Carnaro, drafted with the syndicalist Alceste De Ambris, organised citizens into corporations and declared music a fundamental institution of the state. D'Annunzio's balcony speeches, uniforms, salutes and mass rituals were later copied by [[e:benito-mussolini|Mussolini]]. The town lived on smuggling and piracy while blockaded by [[e:italy|Italy]].
italian-regency-of-carnaro.e: The Treaty of Rapallo in November 1920 made [[s:free-state-of-fiume|Fiume]] a free state. When D'Annunzio refused to accept it, Italian troops and warships attacked in the 'Bloody Christmas' of December 1920, and he left in January 1921. The Free State of Fiume followed.

iron-confederacy.t: The Nehiyaw-Pwat, an alliance of Plains Cree, Assiniboine, Saulteaux and Métis that dominated the northern Plains fur and bison trade until 1885.
iron-confederacy.o: The Cree and the Assiniboine, or Nakoda, had long been allies, and in the 18th century they became the main middlemen between the Hudson's Bay Company posts on [[e:hudson-bay|Hudson Bay]] and peoples of the interior. As they moved west onto the plains and took up horses and bison hunting, Saulteaux and later Métis groups joined them in an alliance the Cree call Nehiyaw-Pwat.
iron-confederacy.r: The confederacy was a military and trading alliance of independent bands, each led by chiefs chosen for skill and generosity, with no central government. Members shared hunting grounds, intermarried and fought together. Guns from the [[e:fur-trade|fur trade]] gave them an early advantage, and they controlled access to trading posts along the Saskatchewan and Red rivers. Their long war with the [[s:blackfoot-confederacy|Blackfoot Confederacy]] from the early 19th century ended with defeat at the Belly River in 1870.
iron-confederacy.e: With the bison vanishing, bands signed Treaty 4 and Treaty 6 with [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]] in 1874 and 1876. Some Cree under Big Bear and Poundmaker were drawn into the North-West Rebellion of 1885, after which the alliance broke up under reserve rule.

imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.t: A Premonstratensian abbey in Swabia whose abbots ruled a small imperial territory between Ulm and Augsburg.
imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.o: Roggenburg was founded in 1126 by the counts of Bibereck as a house of Premonstratensian canons. Raised to an abbey in 1444, it struggled for a century to free itself from outside advocates, and in 1544 its abbots won recognition of imperial immediacy.
imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.r: The abbot governed a compact territory of villages in the hills between the Iller and the Günz as a member of the Swabian Circle and the Swabian bench of prelates. Farming and forestry provided income. Between 1752 and 1758 the canons built a large rococo church, which still stands.
imperial-abbey-of-roggenburg.e: In 1802 the abbey was secularised and annexed by Bavaria, and its library and treasures were dispersed. Premonstratensian canons returned in 1982, and Roggenburg is again a monastery.

igodomigodo-ogiso-dynasty.t: The first Edo kingdom in what is now southern Nigeria, ruled by the Ogisos or 'kings of the sky' before the Oba dynasty of Benin.
igodomigodo-ogiso-dynasty.o: Known almost entirely from Edo oral tradition and archaeology. According to tradition, the Edo villages of the forest west of the lower [[e:niger-river|Niger]] were united under a line of rulers called [[e:ogiso-dynasty|Ogiso]], 'ruler of the sky', the first of whom was Igodo. The kingdom took its name, Igodomigodo, from him, and is traditionally dated from around the 10th century.
igodomigodo-ogiso-dynasty.r: Tradition counts some 31 [[e:ogiso-dynasty|Ogisos]], who ruled with chiefs drawn from the leading lineages, the forerunners of the later [[e:uzama|Uzama]] nobility. Craft [[e:guild|guilds]] in wood and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and the first of the earthen walls around [[e:benin-city|Benin City]] are attributed to this era. Kingship was sacred and tied to Edo religion, ancestor worship and the cult of the land.
igodomigodo-ogiso-dynasty.e: The last [[e:ogiso-dynasty|Ogiso]], Owodo, was banished, and after an interregnum under the administrators Evian and Ogiamien the Edo chiefs invited Prince [[e:oranmiyan|Oranmiyan]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-ife|Kingdom of Ife]]. His son [[e:eweka-i|Eweka I]] founded the [[e:oba-dynasty|Oba dynasty]] around 1180, and Igodomigodo became the [[s:benin-empire|Benin Empire]], which kept many Ogiso-era titles and rituals.

imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.t: A convent founded at the tomb of King Henry the Fowler, whose princess-abbesses, often royal women, ruled Quedlinburg for nearly nine centuries.
imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.o: After King Henry the Fowler died in 936 and was buried at Quedlinburg, his widow Matilda and their son [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] founded a community of canonesses there to pray for him. Otto's daughter Matilda became its first abbess in 966, and while her nephew Otto III was in [[e:italy|Italy]] from 997 she acted as regent in [[e:germany|Germany]].
imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.r: Quedlinburg was a favoured Ottonian palace where emperors celebrated Easter, and its abbesses were princesses of the Empire ruling the town and surrounding lands. The treasure includes Ottonian [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]] and reliquaries, some stolen in 1945 and recovered in 1993. Abbess Anna II introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1539, and later abbesses were Lutheran princesses, often of the Swedish or Prussian royal houses.
imperial-abbey-of-quedlinburg.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. Its last abbess was Sophia Albertina of [[e:sweden|Sweden]]. The collegiate church and castle hill, with [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Henry's]] tomb, are part of the Quedlinburg World Heritage Site.

inalids.t: A Turkmen dynasty that ruled the walled city of Amid (Diyarbakir) for most of the 12th century after the fall of the Marwanids.
inalids.o: After the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]] ended the Marwanid [[e:emirate|emirate]] in the 1080s, a [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] commander named Inal established himself in Amid in the 1090s, founding a small hereditary emirate on the upper [[e:tigris|Tigris]].
inalids.r: The Inalids held little more than Amid and its district and relied on alliances with the [[s:artuqids-of-mardin|Artuqids]] and the [[s:zengid-dynasty|Zengids]]. For long periods real power lay with their [[e:vizier|viziers]] of the Nisanid family, local notables who managed the city. Inscriptions on the great basalt walls of Amid record building work in this period. The population included [[e:kurds|Kurds]], [[e:arabs|Arabs]], [[e:armenians|Armenians]] and [[e:syriac|Syriac]] Christians.
inalids.e: In 1183 [[e:saladin|Saladin]] besieged and took Amid and handed it to his ally, the Artuqid [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] Muhammad, merging it into the [[s:artuqids-of-hasankeyf|Artuqids of Hasankeyf]].

imperial-abbey-of-buchau.t: A house of noble canonesses on the Federsee whose princess-abbesses ruled a small territory of the Holy Roman Empire.
imperial-abbey-of-buchau.o: Tradition credits the founding of the abbey around 770 to Adelindis, a noblewoman linked to the [[e:carolingian-empire|Carolingians]], on an island in the Federsee in upper Swabia. It became a house of secular canonesses drawn only from the high nobility. Its status under the emperor was confirmed in the 14th century, and its abbess came to rank as a princess of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-buchau.r: The princess-abbess sat on the Swabian bench of prelates in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]] and governed villages around the lake and estates elsewhere. The canonesses took no permanent vows and could leave to marry. The neighbouring [[s:free-imperial-city-of-buchau|Free Imperial City of Buchau]] quarrelled with the abbey over rights for centuries. The house remained Catholic.
imperial-abbey-of-buchau.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and, with the town, granted to the princes of [[s:principality-of-thurn-and-taxis|Thurn und Taxis]] as compensation for lost lands. In 1806 the territory passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. The abbey church of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian survives in Bad Buchau.

icelandic-commonwealth.t: Medieval Iceland's kingless republic of chieftains and law assemblies, the society that produced the Icelandic sagas.
icelandic-commonwealth.o: Settlers, mostly from western [[e:norway|Norway]] and the Norse colonies in the British Isles, occupied [[s:republic-of-iceland|Iceland]] from about 870, a period recorded in the Landnámabók. Around 930 they founded the Althing, a general assembly at Þingvellir, which gave the island a [[e:common-law|common law]] without a king.
icelandic-commonwealth.r: Power rested with chieftains, the goðar, whose followers could choose which chieftain to support. A law-speaker recited the law at the Althing, and courts settled disputes, though there was no executive to enforce verdicts. In 1000 the Althing, guided by Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði, adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]]. The Commonwealth produced the sagas, the Eddas and the histories of Snorri Sturluson.
icelandic-commonwealth.e: In the 13th century, the Sturlung Age, a few great families fought for supremacy, and the Norwegian king Haakon IV intervened. In 1262-1264 the Icelanders accepted the Old Covenant, submitting to Norwegian rule, and Gissur Þorvaldsson became earl. [[s:republic-of-iceland|Iceland]] later passed to [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and regained independence as the [[s:kingdom-of-iceland|Kingdom of Iceland]] and Republic of Iceland.

islamic-republic-of-iran.t: The Shia theocratic republic created by the revolution of 1979, in which elected institutions operate under the authority of a Supreme Leader.
islamic-republic-of-iran.o: Mass protests in 1978 brought down [[s:pahlavi-iran|Pahlavi Iran]]. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile on 1 February 1979, and after a referendum the Islamic Republic was proclaimed on 1 April 1979. A constitution adopted in December 1979 enshrined velayat-e faqih, the guardianship of the Islamic jurist.
islamic-republic-of-iran.r: Power is shared between a Supreme Leader, an elected president and parliament, and unelected bodies such as the Guardian Council and the Revolutionary Guards. The early years saw the US embassy hostage crisis of 1979 to 1981, purges of leftists and liberals, and the Iran-[[e:iraq|Iraq]] War of 1980 to 1988. Ali Khamenei became Supreme Leader in 1989. Reformist periods under Mohammad Khatami alternated with crackdowns, including on the Green Movement of 2009 and the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' protests of 2022.
islamic-republic-of-iran.e: The country's nuclear programme led to [[e:sanctions|sanctions]], the 2015 nuclear deal and the US withdrawal from it in 2018, and in 2025 to open war with [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]]. [[e:iran|Iran's]] oil economy, regional alliances and internal dissent continue to shape the state.
