idrisid-emirate-of-asir.t: A Sufi-led emirate on the Red Sea coast of Arabia that rebelled against the Ottomans, allied with Italy and Britain, and was absorbed by Saudi Arabia.
idrisid-emirate-of-asir.o: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi, great-grandson of the Moroccan [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teacher Ahmad ibn Idris, settled at Sabya in the coastal Tihama of Asir. Building on his religious prestige, he rallied the tribes against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire's]] [[s:yemen-vilayet|Yemen Vilayet]] around 1906-1910 and established an independent [[e:emirate|emirate]].
idrisid-emirate-of-asir.r: The Idrisi ruled as a religious reformer and tribal leader, enforcing Islamic law and suppressing feuds. During the [[e:italo-turkish-war|Italo-Turkish War]] [[e:italy|Italy]] supplied him with arms, and in 1915 he signed a treaty with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. After the war [[e:britain|Britain]] handed him the port of Hodeidah in 1921, putting him at odds with [[e:imam|Imam]] Yahya's [[s:mutawakkilite-kingdom-of-yemen|Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen]].
idrisid-emirate-of-asir.e: After Muhammad's death in 1923, succession quarrels weakened the [[e:emirate|emirate]] and Yahya took Hodeidah. In 1926 Hasan al-Idrisi accepted a Saudi [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]; Ibn Saud annexed the territory in 1930, and after a failed revolt and the Saudi-Yemeni war of 1934 it was absorbed into [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]].

independent-state-of-croatia.t: Axis puppet state ruled by Ante Pavelić's Ustaše, notorious for genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma during the Second World War.
independent-state-of-croatia.o: As German forces invaded the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]], the Ustaše leader Slavko Kvaternik proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia in Zagreb on 10 April 1941, ending the [[s:banovina-of-croatia|Banovina of Croatia]]. Ante Pavelić returned from [[e:italy|Italy]] as Poglavnik. The state included Croatia and all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in the [[e:rome|Rome]] Agreements of May 1941 ceded much of [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]] to Italy.
independent-state-of-croatia.r: The Ustaše regime was a one-party dictatorship under German and Italian protection, with a nominal king, the Italian Prince Aimone, as Tomislav II from 1941 to 1943. It pursued the murder, expulsion and forced conversion of [[e:serbs|Serbs]] and the extermination of [[e:jews|Jews]] and Roma, in camps such as Jasenovac. Much of its territory was contested by Partisans and Chetniks.
independent-state-of-croatia.e: As Partisan forces advanced, the state collapsed in May 1945. Its troops and civilians fleeing to [[e:austria|Austria]] were turned back at Bleiburg and many were killed by the Partisans. Pavelić escaped to [[s:argentine-republic|Argentina]]. The territory became part of the [[s:socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia|Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia]].

imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.t: Benedictine abbey on the Swabian Jura that bought its freedom from Württemberg and built one of Germany's great baroque churches.
imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.o: Zwiefalten was founded in 1089 by the counts of Achalm as a Benedictine monastery, settled from Hirsau. For centuries the dukes of Württemberg held its advocacy and pressed claims over it, until the abbey bought its independence in 1750 and became an imperial abbey.
imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.r: The abbot ruled several villages as a prelate of the Empire and sat on the Swabian bench of prelates. Wealth from estates paid for the rebuilding of the abbey church between 1739 and 1765 by Johann Michael Fischer, with stucco by Johann Michael Feichtmayr and frescoes by [[e:franz-joseph-i|Franz Joseph]] Spiegler, a masterpiece of the late baroque.
imperial-abbey-of-zwiefalten.e: In 1802 and 1803 the abbey was secularised and its lands given to the [[s:duchy-of-wurttemberg|Duchy of Württemberg]]. The monastery buildings became a psychiatric hospital in 1812, a role they still fill; the church is now a parish church.

cr.a: Franz Joseph Spiegler / Johann Michael Feuchtmayer

ilmen-slavs.t: The northernmost East Slavs, centred on Lake Ilmen, whose invitation to Rurik began the Rurikid dynasty in the chronicle tradition.
ilmen-slavs.o: [[e:slavs|Slavs]] reached the basin of Lake Ilmen and the Volkhov river in the 7th and 8th centuries, settling among Finnic and Baltic peoples. The chronicles call them the Slovene. Their main centres were the trading settlement of Staraya Ladoga and Rurikovo Gorodishche near the later Novgorod.
ilmen-slavs.r: They lived from farming, fishing, hunting and the [[e:fur-trade|fur trade]], and their territory sat on the routes linking the Baltic with the [[e:volga|Volga]] and the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]]. Scandinavian merchants and warriors were present from the 8th century. The tribe was led by elders and assemblies, which foreshadowed the later town assembly, the veche, of Novgorod.
ilmen-slavs.e: According to the Primary Chronicle, the Slovene, [[s:krivichs|Krivichs]] and Finnic tribes expelled the Varangians and then invited Rurik to rule them in 862. In 882 his successor Oleg moved south to Kiev, and Ilmen became the northern half of [[s:kievan-rus|Kievan Rus']]. Their land developed into the [[s:novgorod-republic|Novgorod Republic]].

imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.t: Benedictine abbey famed for its early medieval library whose prince-abbots ruled north-eastern Switzerland until the French invasion of 1798.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.o: The abbey grew from the cell of the Irish monk Gallus and was founded as a monastery by Otmar in 719. Its scriptorium, library and the Plan of Saint Gall made it a centre of Carolingian learning. Its abbots gained wide estates, and from 1206 they were recognised as princes of the Empire.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.r: The prince-abbots governed lands around Lake Constance and the Thur, but lost [[s:canton-of-appenzell|Appenzell]] in the Appenzell Wars and clashed with the city of St. Gallen. Abbot Ulrich Rösch rebuilt their power, buying the [[s:county-of-toggenburg|County of Toggenburg]] in 1468 and allying with the [[s:old-swiss-confederacy|Old Swiss Confederacy]]. The abbey remained Catholic, while the city and parts of Toggenburg turned Protestant. Its baroque church and library were built in the 1750s and 1760s.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-gall.e: The French invasion of 1798 and the [[s:helvetic-republic|Helvetic Republic]] ended its secular rule, and the abbey was dissolved in 1805. Its lands became the canton of St. Gallen in 1803. The abbey precinct and library are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

idel-ural-state.t: A Tatar-Bashkir national state proclaimed on the Volga in 1918 and suppressed by the Bolsheviks within weeks.
idel-ural-state.o: After the [[e:february-revolution|February Revolution]], Muslim congresses in Kazan and Ufa debated autonomy for the [[e:turkic-peoples|Turkic peoples]] of the [[e:volga|Volga]] and Urals. In late 1917 the National Assembly of Muslims of Inner [[e:russia|Russia]] and [[e:siberia|Siberia]] resolved to create the Idel-Ural State, uniting [[e:tatars|Tatars]], Bashkirs and Chuvash, with Kazan as capital, and its proclamation was planned for March 1918.
idel-ural-state.r: The project was led by [[e:tatars|Tatar]] politicians such as Sadri Maqsudi and Galimjan Sharaf, envisaging a democratic federal state with Muslim institutions and minority rights. It had a militia based in the Tatar quarter of Kazan, across the Bulaq canal, known as the 'Zabulachnaya Republic', but almost no administration beyond the city.
idel-ural-state.e: Bolshevik forces arrested its leaders in Kazan in February 1918 and dispersed the defenders of the [[e:tatars|Tatar]] quarter in March, ending the state. The Soviets later created the Tatar ASSR in 1920. The Idel-Ural idea survived among Tatar émigrés.

idar-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state in the hills of north-eastern Gujarat, ruled by a branch of the Jodhpur royal house.
idar-state.o: Idar had an older line of Rao chiefs, but in 1728 Anand Singh and Rai Singh, brothers of Maharaja Abhai Singh of Jodhpur, took the fortress with Mughal sanction and founded a new Rathore dynasty. [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] pressure soon forced it to pay tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda State]].
idar-state.r: Idar was the leading state of the Mahi Kantha Agency, governed by a Maharaja over hilly, partly tribal country. Its most famous ruler was Sir Pratap Singh of Jodhpur, the soldier and friend of the British royal family, who held Idar from 1902 to 1911. The town of Ahmednagar, which became the capital, was later renamed Himmatnagar after Maharaja Himmat Singh (ruled 1931–49).
idar-state.e: Idar acceded to [[e:india|India]] and in 1948 was merged into Bombay State; since 1960 its lands, centred on Himmatnagar, are in Sabarkantha district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.t: A royal Carolingian abbey near Worms, famous for its gatehouse, its library and the Lorsch Codex, a vast record of medieval land grants.
imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.o: Lorsch was founded in 764 by the Frankish count Cancor and his mother Williswinda, and handed to Archbishop Chrodegang of Metz. Relics of the Roman martyr Saint Nazarius drew pilgrims and gifts. In 772 [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] made it a royal abbey, giving it imperial protection and immunity.
imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.r: Lorsch grew into one of the richest abbeys of the Frankish realm, with thousands of donations recorded in the 12th-century Lorsch Codex. Its library held important classical and Christian [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]], and the Lorsch Pharmacopoeia is a key early medical text. The East Frankish king [[e:louis-the-german|Louis the German]] and his son Louis the Younger were buried there.
imperial-abbey-of-lorsch.e: Decline came in the 12th century with disputes over its lands. In 1232 Emperor [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] gave Lorsch to the Archbishop of [[e:mainz|Mainz]], ending its independence; the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]] later took control. Its gatehouse, the Königshalle, survives and is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.t: One of the oldest and richest abbeys of the Rhineland, outside Trier, whose long fight to stay independent of the archbishops ended in 1669.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.o: Saint Maximin's Abbey grew around the tomb of [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Maximin of [[e:trier|Trier]] in the 4th century and became a Benedictine abbey. It was richly endowed by Frankish kings and became an imperial abbey. In 1139 King Conrad III placed it under the Archbishop of Trier, beginning centuries of dispute over its status.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.r: The abbey held extensive estates in the Moselle region and [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]] and was a centre of the 10th-century Gorze reform movement. Its abbots claimed to be princes of the Empire with lands of their own, while the archbishops of [[e:trier|Trier]] claimed the abbey as their territory, fighting the case in imperial courts.
imperial-abbey-of-saint-maximin.e: In 1669 the Imperial Aulic Council confirmed the Archbishop of [[e:trier|Trier's]] lordship, ending the abbey's claim to independence. The abbey was dissolved under French rule in 1802; its rebuilt church survives in Trier as a school and event hall.

iceni.t: East Anglian kingdom whose queen Boudica led the great revolt of 60 or 61, burning Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before Rome crushed the rising.
iceni.o: The Iceni held Norfolk and parts of Suffolk and Cambridgeshire; they are probably the Cenimagni who surrendered to [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] in 54 BCE. In the 1st century BCE their elite deposited spectacular gold torcs at Snettisham, and from about 10 BCE they issued [[e:silver|silver]] coins, some inscribed ECEN, with horse designs.
iceni.r: Coins name rulers such as Antedios, and settlements like Thetford and Saham Toney appear to have been major centres. After the Roman conquest of 43 the Iceni became a client kingdom, but they rebelled in 47 when the governor Ostorius Scapula tried to disarm them. Prasutagus later ruled as a client king, enjoying Roman favour while keeping horse-rearing and an independent elite.
iceni.e: When Prasutagus died around 60, leaving half his realm to Nero, Roman officials seized it, flogged his widow Boudica and raped her daughters. Boudica led the Iceni and [[s:trinovantes|Trinovantes]] in revolt and destroyed three cities before Suetonius Paulinus defeated her. The territory was annexed and later organised as a civitas centred on Venta Icenorum.

iapydes.t: Warlike people of the Lika and Una highlands in modern Croatia and Bosnia, blending Illyrian and Celtic culture until Octavian crushed them.
iapydes.o: The Iapydes formed in the hinterland of the northern Adriatic during the Iron Age, around the 6th century BCE, in the Lika plateau and the Una valley near Bihać. Their material culture developed from local [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] traditions, with growing Celtic influence from the 4th century BCE.
iapydes.r: They lived in hillforts led by local chiefs, with Metulum as their main stronghold. They are known for stone cinerary urns carved with reliefs, distinctive bronze headgear and amber jewellery. Herding and raiding into the Roman province of [[e:italy|Italy]] and on Aquileia brought them into conflict with [[e:rome|Rome]]; a campaign under Sempronius Tuditanus defeated them in 129 BCE.
iapydes.e: In 35 BCE Octavian led his Illyrian campaign against them; at the siege of Metulum he was wounded and the defenders burned their town rather than surrender. The Iapydes were subdued by 34 BCE and absorbed into the province of Illyricum.

italiote-league.t: Alliance of the Greek cities of southern Italy against the Lucanians and the tyrants of Syracuse, later led by Taras until the Roman conquest.
italiote-league.o: The Greek cities of southern [[e:italy|Italy]], the Italiotes, drew together in the late 5th century BCE as Oscan-speaking [[s:lucanians|Lucanians]] pressed on their territory and [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] grew ambitious. The Achaean cities, led by [[s:croton|Croton]], formed the core, with a common sanctuary at the temple of Hera Lacinia near Croton.
italiote-league.r: Members pledged to help any city attacked by the [[s:lucanians|Lucanians]], and Diodorus says the generals of a city that failed to send help were to be put to death. Its army was defeated by the Lucanians near Laus in 389 BCE and, in the same year, by Dionysius I at the Elleporus river, after which he dismantled [[s:kaulonia|Kaulonia]] and [[s:hipponion|Hipponion]]. In the mid-4th century BCE [[s:taras|Taras]] took the lead and moved the league's seat to [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]], hiring generals from [[e:greece|Greece]].
italiote-league.e: Under Tarentine leadership the league drew in Pyrrhus against [[e:rome|Rome]] in 280 BCE. After his departure and the surrender of [[s:taras|Taras]] in 272 BCE, the Greek cities became separate allies of Rome and the league ceased to exist.

ijesha-kingdom.t: Yoruba kingdom of the eastern uplands centred on Ilesa, whose war leader Ogedengbe led the Ekiti Parapo against Ibadan.
ijesha-kingdom.o: Ijesha tradition holds that the kingdom was founded by Ajibogun, called Obokun, a son of [[e:oduduwa|Oduduwa]] who fetched sea water to cure his father's blindness and was rewarded with a crown. His title, Owa Obokun, became that of the kings of Ijesha, who later fixed their capital at Ilesa.
ijesha-kingdom.r: The Owa ruled with a council of town chiefs and war chiefs over farming communities in a fertile hill country. Ijesha was a regional power among the eastern [[e:yoruba|Yoruba]], trading kola and cloth. In the 19th century [[e:ibadan|Ibadan's]] expansion brought defeat and occupation, and the Ijesha warlord Ogedengbe rose to lead resistance.
ijesha-kingdom.e: Ijesha joined the [[s:ekiti-parapo|Ekiti Parapo]] alliance in the long Kiriji war against [[s:ibadan|Ibadan]] from 1877, until a British-brokered treaty of 1886 halted the fighting and the war camps were dispersed in 1893. It then came under British control within [[s:protectorate-of-southern-nigeria|Southern Nigeria]], and the Owa Obokun still reigns at Ilesa in Osun State.

idrisid-dynasty.t: The first Islamic dynasty to rule much of Morocco, founded by a descendant of the Prophet who built the city of Fez.
idrisid-dynasty.o: Idris ibn Abd Allah, a great-grandson of [[e:hasan-ibn-ali|Hasan ibn Ali]], fled [[e:arabia|Arabia]] after a failed Alid revolt at Fakhkh in 786. In 788 the Awraba [[e:berbers|Berbers]] of Volubilis, heirs to the [[s:kingdom-of-altava|Kingdom of Altava]], recognised him as [[e:imam|imam]]. He conquered much of northern [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]] and founded a town on the [[e:fez|Fez]] river before being poisoned, reportedly by an Abbasid agent, in 791.
idrisid-dynasty.r: His posthumous son Idris II made [[e:fez|Fez]] a capital, settling refugees from [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] and [[e:kairouan|Kairouan]] in its two quarters. The Idrisids spread [[e:islam|Islam]] and Arabic among [[e:berbers|Berber]] tribes and gave Moroccan Islam its tradition of sharifian descent. In 859 [[e:fatima|Fatima]] al-Fihri founded the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez. After 828 the realm was divided among Idris II's sons, and the [[s:sulaymanid-emirate|Sulaymanid emirate]] held [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]].
idrisid-dynasty.e: In the 10th century the Idrisids were caught between the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] and the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. The last emir, al-Hasan ibn Kannun, surrendered to [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] in 974 and was later killed. Idrisid descent remained prestigious, and the tomb of Idris II is a national shrine.

imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.t: A wealthy Benedictine abbey in upper Swabia that broke free of Saint Blasien and ruled one of the largest monastic territories in the region.
imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.o: Founded around 1090 as a priory of the Black Forest abbey of Saint Blasien, Ochsenhausen became an independent abbey in 1391. In 1495 it was freed from outside advocates and recognised as an imperial abbey, with its abbot sitting among the Swabian prelates of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.r: The abbot ruled several dozen villages, making Ochsenhausen one of the largest monastic territories in Swabia. Its peasants rose against the abbey in 1502 and again in the Peasants' War of 1525. In the 18th century the monks rebuilt their church and buildings in Baroque style, and Joseph Gabler built a celebrated organ for the church in the 1720s and 1730s.
imperial-abbey-of-ochsenhausen.e: In 1803 the abbey was secularised and given to Count Franz Georg von Metternich, father of the Austrian chancellor, as compensation for lands lost west of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. It passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806, and the Metternichs sold their rights there in 1825.

imperial-abbey-of-lindau.t: A house of noble canonesses on an island in Lake Constance whose princess-abbesses ruled a tiny territory beside the free city of Lindau.
imperial-abbey-of-lindau.o: The women's community on the island of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-lindau|Lindau]] was founded in the 9th century, and the town that grew up beside it became a free imperial city. The abbey's direct dependence on the empire was confirmed in the 15th century, and its abbess ranked as a princess of the empire.
imperial-abbey-of-lindau.r: The canonesses were noblewomen who lived without permanent vows. The princess-abbess governed scattered villages and rights around Lake Constance, but the abbey was entangled in long disputes with the city of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-lindau|Lindau]], which adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1520s, while the abbey remained Catholic.
imperial-abbey-of-lindau.e: In 1802 and 1803 the abbey was secularised and granted to the princes of Bretzenheim, who soon exchanged it; it passed to [[e:austria|Austria]] and in 1805 to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. The former abbey buildings stand in Lindau's old town.

indo-parthian-kingdom.t: The realm of Gondophares, a Parthian king who ruled Gandhara and Sistan and whom Christian legend linked with the Apostle Thomas.
indo-parthian-kingdom.o: Gondophares, a ruler of Iranian, probably Parthian, origin from Sistan, built a kingdom in the early 1st century by taking [[e:arachosia|Arachosia]] and then [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Gandhara]] and [[e:taxila|Taxila]] from the [[s:indo-scythians|Indo-Scythians]]. The Takht-i-Bahi inscription in Gandhara is dated to the 26th year of his reign, around 46.
indo-parthian-kingdom.r: The Indo-Parthian kings continued [[e:indo-greek-kingdom|Indo-Greek]] and [[s:saka|Saka]] traditions of bilingual coinage with Greek and Kharoshthi legends and ruled through governors and allied local dynasties such as the [[s:apracharajas|Apracharajas]]. Buddhist monasteries flourished, including Takht-i-Bahi. The apocryphal Acts of Thomas tell how the Apostle Thomas came to the court of King Gudnaphar, a name matching Gondophares; the Greek sage Apollonius reportedly visited [[e:taxila|Taxila]] under a Parthian king.
indo-parthian-kingdom.e: After Gondophares the kingdom split among successors such as Abdagases and Pacores. In the later 1st century the [[s:kushan-empire|Kushan Empire]] took [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Gandhara]] and [[e:taxila|Taxila]]. Indo-Parthian rulers survived in Sistan and Baluchistan until the rise of the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] around 226.

ichalkaranji-state.t: A Maratha jagir of the Deccan held by the Ghorpade family under Kolhapur, its town now a major textile centre.
ichalkaranji-state.o: Ichalkaranji was granted at the end of the 17th century to Naro Mahadev, a [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] officer whose descendants took the name Ghorpade. The family held it as a feudatory of [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur State]].
ichalkaranji-state.r: The chiefs ruled a small territory on the Panchganga river, subordinate to [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] and under British supervision through the Kolhapur residency. In the early 20th century the town began to develop handloom and powerloom weaving.
ichalkaranji-state.e: Ichalkaranji merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1949 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960. It is now one of Maharashtra's leading textile towns, in [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] district.

imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.t: A Benedictine abbey in the Swabian Allgäu, founded in 764, whose abbots ruled a small territory and built one of Germany's grandest Baroque churches.
imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.o: Founded in 764 by the Swabian noble Silach and protected by [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]], the abbey built up lands in the Günz valley. From the 13th century the prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] held its advocacy, and the abbots spent centuries asserting their independence; only in 1710 did the abbey buy out [[e:augsburg|Augsburg's]] rights and secure full imperial immediacy.
imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.r: The abbot ruled several villages as a member of the Swabian Circle and of the prelates' bench of the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]]. Income from farms, forests and tithes paid for learning and building: from 1711 Abbot Rupert Ness rebuilt the monastery, and under Anselm Erb the great church was completed to designs by Johann Michael Fischer, a masterpiece of south German Baroque.
imperial-abbey-of-ottobeuren.e: The abbey was secularised in 1802 and its territory annexed by the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]]. Monks returned in 1834, and Ottobeuren is again a Benedictine community whose basilica and organs draw many visitors.

islamic-republic-of-afghanistan.t: The Western-backed Afghan state that followed the Taliban's fall in 2001, holding elections and expanding education before collapsing in 2021.
islamic-republic-of-afghanistan.o: After the US-led invasion overthrew the [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001|Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan]] (1996-2001), the Bonn Agreement of December 2001 created an interim administration under Hamid Karzai. A loya jirga approved a new constitution in 2004, establishing the Islamic [[s:democratic-republic-of-afghanistan|Republic of Afghanistan]], and Karzai was elected president.
islamic-republic-of-afghanistan.r: The republic held presidential and parliamentary elections and expanded schools, healthcare and media, with millions of girls returning to school. It depended on foreign aid and NATO forces, including the ISAF mission. Corruption, disputed elections, opium production and a growing Taliban insurgency weakened it. Ashraf Ghani succeeded Karzai in 2014, sharing power with Abdullah Abdullah.
islamic-republic-of-afghanistan.e: After the US-Taliban Doha agreement of 2020 and the withdrawal of foreign troops, the Taliban took provincial capitals rapidly. Ghani fled on 15 August 2021, [[e:kabul|Kabul]] fell, and the [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-1996-2001|Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan]] (2021-present) was restored.

imperial-city-of-besancon.t: A free city of the Holy Roman Empire inside Franche-Comté, ruled by its citizens rather than its archbishops until Louis XIV took it in 1674.
imperial-city-of-besancon.o: Besançon was an ancient archbishopric whose archbishops long held authority in the city. After repeated revolts, the citizens obtained recognition of their liberties, and in 1290 Rudolf of [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] confirmed the city as a free imperial city, separate from the surrounding [[s:free-county-of-burgundy|Free County of Burgundy]].
imperial-city-of-besancon.r: The city was governed by elected governors and councillors drawn from its wards, while the archbishop kept spiritual and some ceremonial rights. It traded across the Jura and the Saône valley. In the 16th century Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, chancellor of [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]], built his palace there, and the city was closely tied to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]].
imperial-city-of-besancon.e: In 1654 the emperor ceded Besançon to [[e:spain|Spain]], joining it to [[s:free-county-of-burgundy|Franche-Comté]]. [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] took the city in 1674, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678 made it French. It became the capital of Franche-Comté, and Vauban built its citadel.

ireland.t: The sovereign Irish state established under the 1937 Constitution, which became a republic in 1949 and an EU member in 1973.
ireland.o: The Constitution of Ireland, drafted under Eamon de Valera and approved by referendum in 1937, replaced the [[s:irish-free-state|Irish Free State]] with a state named Ireland, or Eire, with an elected President, Douglas Hyde being the first. It claimed the whole island but applied its laws to twenty-six counties.
ireland.r: Ireland stayed neutral in the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] and declared itself a republic in 1949, leaving the Commonwealth. It is a parliamentary democracy with the Oireachtas and a Taoiseach. Long dominated by the Catholic Church and emigration, it changed through economic openness, EEC membership in 1973 and the 'Celtic Tiger' boom of the 1990s.
ireland.e: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 replaced its territorial claim with an aspiration to unity by consent. Referendums legalised divorce, same-sex marriage in 2015 and abortion in 2018, and Ireland is a member of the eurozone.

ikhshidid-emirate.t: An autonomous dynasty that ruled Egypt, Syria and the holy cities under Abbasid sovereignty, ending with the regent Kafur.
ikhshidid-emirate.o: Muhammad ibn Tughj, a commander of Central Asian descent from Farghana, became governor of [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in 935 and restored order after years of turmoil. In 939 the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] granted him the old princely title al-Ikhshid, which gave the dynasty its name, while he ruled as an autonomous emir of the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]].
ikhshidid-emirate.r: The Ikhshidids governed from [[e:fustat|Fustat]] and held southern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Hejaz]], including [[e:mecca|Mecca]] and [[e:medina|Medina]], contesting northern [[e:syria|Syria]] with the Hamdanids. After al-Ikhshid died in 946, real power passed to Abu al-Misk Kafur, a [[e:eunuch|eunuch]] of African origin, who ran the state as regent for two sons and ruled in his own name from 966. The poet al-Mutanabbi spent time at his court, first praising and then lampooning him.
ikhshidid-emirate.e: After Kafur's death in 968, famine and factional strife left [[e:egypt|Egypt]] open to attack. In 969 the Fatimid general [[s:jawhar-state|Jawhar]] entered [[e:fustat|Fustat]] almost unopposed and founded [[e:cairo|Cairo]] nearby, bringing Egypt into the [[s:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimid Caliphate]].

indo-scythians.t: Saka nomads from Central Asia who took over north-western India from the Greeks and founded lines of satraps that ruled for centuries.
indo-scythians.o: The [[s:saka|Sakas]], Scythian nomads of [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]], were driven south by the [[s:yuezhi|Yuezhi]] in the 2nd century BCE. They passed through Sistan and [[e:arachosia|Arachosia]] into the [[e:indus|Indus]] valley. Around 85 BCE their king Maues established himself in [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Gandhara]] and took [[e:taxila|Taxila]] from the [[s:indo-greek-kingdom|Indo-Greek Kingdom]], founding a Saka kingdom in north-western [[e:india|India]].
indo-scythians.r: Indo-Scythian kings called themselves [[e:negus-nagast|king of kings]] and copied [[e:indo-greek-kingdom|Indo-Greek]] coinage, with Greek and Kharoshthi legends. They ruled through [[e:satrapy|satraps]], provincial governors who often became hereditary rulers. Under Azes I, whose era beginning in 57 BCE was used in inscriptions, the kingdom spread over [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Gandhara]] and the [[e:punjab|Punjab]]. They patronised [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]], as the Bimaran reliquary and the Mathura Lion Capital show, and [[e:taxila|Taxila's]] city at Sirkap flourished.
indo-scythians.e: In the early 1st century the [[s:indo-parthian-kingdom|Indo-Parthian Kingdom]] under Gondophares took over [[e:taxila|Taxila]] and [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Gandhara]]. [[s:saka|Saka]] [[e:satrapy|satraps]] survived elsewhere, among them the [[s:northern-satraps|Northern Satraps]] of Mathura and the [[s:western-satraps|Western Satraps]], who ruled western [[e:india|India]] until about 415.

ikshvaku-dynasty.t: Successors of the Satavahanas in the Krishna valley, whose queens funded the great Buddhist monasteries of Nagarjunakonda.
ikshvaku-dynasty.o: The Ikshvakus, claiming descent from the legendary solar dynasty, rose in the lower Krishna valley of Andhra as the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Satavahana dynasty]] collapsed in the early 3rd century. Their founder, Vasishthiputra Chamtamula, built the capital Vijayapuri in the valley now called Nagarjunakonda.
ikshvaku-dynasty.r: The kings performed Vedic sacrifices, including the horse sacrifice, while the women of the royal house and their relatives were lavish patrons of [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]]. Inscriptions record their gifts to stupas and monasteries at Nagarjunakonda, which hosted monks from [[s:sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]] and elsewhere. The site's limestone carvings belong to the Amaravati school. King Virapurushadatta married into the [[s:western-satraps|Western Satraps]]' family.
ikshvaku-dynasty.e: Ikshvaku rule ended in the early 4th century, probably through the expansion of the [[s:pallava-dynasty|Pallava dynasty]] and the [[s:abhira-dynasty|Abhira dynasty]]. Vijayapuri was flooded by the Nagarjuna Sagar dam in the 1960s, after excavated monuments were moved to higher ground.

irish-free-state.t: The self-governing dominion of twenty-six Irish counties established by the Anglo-Irish Treaty in 1922, the forerunner of modern Ireland.
irish-free-state.o: The Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 created the Irish Free State as a dominion of the British Commonwealth, with the British monarch as head of state and an oath of fidelity. It came into being on 6 December 1922, during the civil war between pro-Treaty and anti-Treaty republicans.
irish-free-state.r: The Free State's first government under W. T. Cosgrave won the civil war in 1923, built a civil service, an unarmed police force, the Garda Siochana, and the Shannon hydroelectric scheme. It joined the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] in 1923. Eamon de Valera's Fianna Fail took power in 1932 and dismantled Treaty links, removing the oath and fighting an economic war with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
irish-free-state.e: A new constitution, approved by referendum in 1937, replaced the Free State with Ireland, or Eire.

ilercavones.t: The Iberian people of the lower Ebro around Tortosa, near whose town Hibera the Scipios defeated Hasdrubal Barca in 215 BCE.
ilercavones.o: The Ilercavones lived around the mouth and lower course of the [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]], in southern [[s:principality-of-catalonia|Catalonia]] and northern Castellón, from about the 5th century BCE. Their position on the river made them a crossroads between the Iberian peoples of the north-east and those of [[e:valencia|Valencia]].
ilercavones.r: Little is known of their government. Their towns included Hibera, near modern Tortosa, and they lived from farming, fishing and trade along the river and coast. They minted coins with Iberian legends, and later the Roman town of Dertosa issued coins naming Hibera Iulia Ilercavonia.
ilercavones.e: In 215 BCE the Scipio brothers defeated Hasdrubal [[s:barca|Barca]] near Hibera, securing the [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] for [[e:rome|Rome]]. The Ilercavones were pacified by 197 BCE and absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]], with Dertosa becoming their main Roman town.

ibadan.t: A Yoruba city-state founded as a war camp, ruled by soldiers rather than kings, which became the strongest military power in 19th-century Yorubaland.
ibadan.o: Ibadan grew around 1829 from a camp of [[e:oyo-empire|Oyo]], [[e:ife|Ife]] and [[s:ijebu-kingdom|Ijebu]] soldiers who had destroyed the town of Owu, amid the wars that followed the collapse of the [[s:oyo-empire|Oyo Empire]]. Refugees and warriors flocked to the site, and within a generation it was one of the largest towns in [[e:west-africa|West Africa]].
ibadan.r: Ibadan had no crowned king. Chiefly titles in civil and military lines, headed by the Baale and the Balogun, were won by success in war and wealth in followers, making it a kind of military republic. Its victory over the [[s:ilorin-emirate|Ilorin Emirate]] at Osogbo around 1840 halted the [[e:fula|Fulani]] advance, and leaders such as Oluyole and Ogunmola built an empire over the [[s:ijesha-kingdom|Ijesha]] and Ekiti.
ibadan.e: Ibadan's dominance provoked the [[s:ekiti-parapo|Ekiti Parapo]] revolt and the Kiriji war of 1877-1893, ended by British mediation. A treaty of 1893 placed Ibadan under British protection, and it became one of [[e:nigeria|Nigeria's]] largest cities.

italia-social-war-confederation.t: Rebel state formed by Rome's Italian allies in the Social War of 91–88 BCE, with its own capital, senate, consuls and coinage.
italia-social-war-confederation.o: For two centuries [[e:rome|Rome's]] Italian allies supplied soldiers for its wars without full citizenship. When the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus, who proposed giving it to them, was murdered in 91 BCE, the [[s:marsi|Marsi]], [[s:paeligni|Paeligni]], [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]], [[s:picentes|Picentes]] and other peoples rose in revolt, starting with a massacre of [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] at Asculum.
italia-social-war-confederation.r: The rebels set up a federal state modelled on [[e:rome|Rome]], with Corfinium as its capital, renamed Italia, a senate of 500 members and two consuls, the Marsian Quintus Poppaedius Silo and the Samnite Gaius Papius Mutilus. They minted [[e:silver|silver]] coins, some inscribed in Oscan as Víteliú, showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf. Their armies, trained in Roman methods, fought Rome on equal terms in 90 BCE.
italia-social-war-confederation.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] divided the rebels by granting citizenship to loyal allies in 90 BCE and to all who laid down arms in 89 BCE. Sulla, Pompeius Strabo and Marius defeated the remaining forces, and Silo was killed in 88 BCE. Within a generation all free Italians south of the Po were Roman citizens.

irish-republic.t: The revolutionary republic declared in 1916 and established by Dail Eireann in 1919, which fought the War of Independence against British rule.
irish-republic.o: The Easter Rising of 1916 proclaimed an Irish Republic. After Sinn Fein won most Irish seats in the 1918 general election, its members met in Dublin on 21 January 1919 as Dail Eireann, adopted a Declaration of Independence and created a government, with Eamon de Valera as president from April 1919.
irish-republic.r: The republic built a counter-state: Dail courts, a loan raised by Michael Collins, local councils and the Irish Republican Army, which fought the War of Independence against British forces from 1919 to 1921. It was recognised by no foreign government.
irish-republic.e: After the truce of July 1921, the Anglo-Irish Treaty, approved by the Dail in January 1922, replaced the republic with the [[s:irish-free-state|Irish Free State]], a dominion. The split over the Treaty led to the Irish Civil War.
